The Long-tailed Jaeger (Stercorarius longicaudus) is a slender, elegant seabird of the high Arctic tundra, exhibiting a life-history strategy finely tuned to its short, intense breeding season. Captive incubation trials have demonstrated that when eggs are maintained at a constant 36 °C [T = 36 °C], hatching occurs after approximately 23 days [ab = approximately 23 days], a period consistent with the developmental rates of other small skua species. The chicks emerge with a wet weight at birth of about 24 grams [Wwb = about 24 grams], a mass that is relatively modest given the species' ultimate adult size but which provides a sufficient nutrient reserve for the initial days of parental brooding. This low birth weight marks the beginning of a rapid growth phase, as the altricial downy chicks must develop quickly to fledge within the narrow window of summer prey abundance. The thermal regime during incubation appears to be critical; temperatures deviating significantly from this optimal value can prolong the incubation period or reduce hatching success, underscoring the importance of consistent parental attendance on the exposed tundra nest.

Under the typical active metabolic conditions for this species, characterized by a body temperature near 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], the fledging milestone is achieved remarkably early. This brief nestling period is among the shortest recorded for birds of comparable body mass, and it is followed by a protracted phase of post-fledging care during which the parents continue to provision the juvenile. The ultimate wet weight of an adult, reached after several months of independent foraging, typically stabilizes around 270 grams [Wwi = around 270 grams], although field records indicate considerable individual variation, with some large individuals exceeding 400 grams depending on prey availability in the preceding winter. This adult mass represents a more than tenfold increase from the initial hatching weight, reflecting the intense somatic growth that must be compressed into a few short summer months.

The pace of sexual development in the Long-tailed Jaeger is likewise constrained by the brevity of the Arctic summer. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal maturation, is attained at roughly 75 days after hatching [tp = roughly 75 days after hatching] when individuals are maintained at a body temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This age is notably delayed relative to the fledging event, indicating that considerable time and energetic investment are required for the completion of structural growth before the reproductive system can activate. Many first-year birds are observed on the breeding grounds in a sub-adult plumage, suggesting that while the physiological machinery for reproduction is in place, full behavioral competence and territory acquisition may take additional time. This relatively short interval to puberty is comparable to that of other Arctic-breeding shorebirds and skuas, where the relentless seasonal clock imposes a premium on rapid development. The synchronization of gonadal recrudescence with the spring thaw is likely mediated by photoperiod, ensuring that hormonal activation aligns with peak lemming and small bird availability.

First reproduction in the Long-tailed Jaeger is a deferred event, typically occurring three years after hatching [tR = three years after hatching] under thermal conditions approximating 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This long prereproductive period is a common feature among long-lived seabirds, reflecting the time needed to acquire the foraging proficiency and social status necessary to secure a nesting territory on the competitive tundra. The maximum recorded lifespan for this species, based on field studies and banding returns, is approximately 3710 days [am = approximately 3710 days], although most individuals likely survive for a shorter duration due to the hazards of migration and winter at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C] storms at sea. This combination of delayed maturity and extended longevity places the species firmly within a slow life-history continuum, typical of many pelagic and Arctic birds. The annual survival rate of adults is thought to be high, with mortality concentrated in the first year of life when inexperienced juveniles face the greatest challenges during their first southward migration to wintering grounds in the Southern Hemisphere.

The reproductive output of the Long-tailed Jaeger is modest but steady over its long adult life. Females typically lay a single clutch of two eggs annually [Ri = a single clutch of two eggs annually]. The maximum daily reproduction rate of the species is thus equivalent to two eggs per 365 days, a value that aligns with its K-selected life history strategy. The eggs are laid in a simple scrape on the tundra, and both parents share incubation responsibilities. This low reproductive rate is balanced by the high survival probability of the long-lived adults, a classic trade-off in birds with extended lifespans. The timing of egg-laying is tightly synchronized with the emergence of Arctic lemmings, which form a critical food source for the provisioning parents and growing chicks. In years of low lemming abundance, the jaegers may forgo breeding entirely, a flexible strategy that conserves adult condition for more favorable future seasons. The relatively large egg size, combined with the efficient two-egg clutch, ensures that each offspring receives substantial maternal investment, enhancing its chances of surviving the perilous first weeks of life and eventual recruitment into the breeding population.
